title: How to Treat Rosacea
caption:
Back with another very commonly asked question, something we see every day in my practice: how to treat rosacea.

#rosacea #dermatologist #skincare #facecare
transcript: Rosacea is a condition where we see redness on the face, usually central facial redness, so around the nose, forehead, chin, and it can be accompanied with acne bumps as well. And there are considered to be four types of rosacea. There's the erythematotelangiectatic type, which is just straight up redness, and then there's the papulopustular rosacea, so the rosacea that gets a lot of acne bumps associated with it. There's ocular rosacea, so you can get rosacea in your eyes, and then there's something called rhinophyma, where people get like a buildup of sebaceous tissue in their nose. like pretty big noses. When it comes to just basic skin care with rosacea, the main thing is just keeping things gentle. Gentle cleansers, gentle moisturizers, gentle sunscreens. I recommend mineral-based sunscreens over chemical sunscreens. Brands that I really like that have gentle cleansing ingredients are CeraVe, La Roche-Posay, Avène, and Aveeno, as well as their moisturizers.

caption: Can you ACTUALLY eat your skincare? Stay to the end for my honest take.
on_screen_hook: Can you actually eat your skincare? Well, kind of. Now, there's no
transcript: Can you actually eat your skincare? Well, kind of. Now, there's no evidence whatsoever that eating carrots will deliver any meaningful amount of retinoid activity to your skin the way, like topical tretinoin or retinol does. But we actually have some decent human studies to show that certain foods and supplements can actually affect the way our skin ages. So, for example, tomatoes, which have lycopene, can actually increase your skin's resistance to UV damage. There's also cocoa, flavanols and other polyphenols that may help with things like elasticity and, like, photo Protection. And then oral collagen peptides do have some decent amount of data. I mean, a lot of its industry back, but they do have studies showing modest improvement in wrinkles, hydration, and elasticity after about three months of use. And then there's also some interesting data with things like green tea, astaxanthin and Omega threes. And we have some emerging data coming out with things like curcumin and resveratrol. But, and this is very important, none of these foods are gonna replace your tried and true skincare. Products like sunscreen, retinoids, and antioxidant serums like vitamin C have decades of research to show its impact on skin health and wrinkles and photo damage. Obviously, nutrition is really important to support your skin from the inside out. But I would not rely on diet alone to make your skin better.
